headlines.title: Nvidia's 7-week losing streak is longest since 2008 financial crisis
headlines.summary: Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now ranks third behind Apple and Microsoft.
headlines.article_text: Nvidia's 7-week losing streak is longest since 2008 financial crisis Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Nvidia shares fell nearly 10% on Friday, and headed for its seventh straight weekly drop. The stock is down 44% over the period, shedding $2.5 trillion in market cap. Once the most valuable company, Nvidia is now fourth behind Apple, Microsoft and Google. In this article NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT People walk past the sign outside the Nvidia corporation office building, Nov. 16, 2026 in Taipei City, Taiwan. Stephen J. Boitano | Lightrocket | Getty Images The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis. Nvidia shares fell nearly 10% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock is poised to close lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008. Shares of Nvidia are down 44% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by $2.5 trillion. The stock is now trading at around 9.3 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months. Once the most valuable company, now, at a market cap of $3.2 trillion, Nvidia is fourth behind Apple and Microsoft and Alphabet . Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy. Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD. Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere. On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December. For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT. Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.
